{{Otheruseslist|{{ill|Atami Onsen in Shizuoka|qid=Q135502389}}|{{ill|Atami Onsen in Fukushima|qid=Q135502391}}|磐梯熱海温泉|{{ill|Atami Onsen in Oita|qid=Q135502394}}|あたみ温泉}}
'''Atami Onsen''' (熱海温泉【あたみおんせん】) is a hot spring located in {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|qid=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture}}’s {{ill|Atami|ar|أتامي (شيزوكا)|arz|اتامى|azb|آتامی، شیزوئوکا|ce|Атами|ceb|Atami (lungsod sa Hapon)|cs|Atami (Šizuoka)|cy|Atami|de|Atami (Shizuoka)|es|Atami|et|Atami|eu|Atami|fa|آتامی، شیزوئوکا|fi|Atami|fr|Atami|gl|Atami|he|אטאמי|hy|Աթամի|id|Atami, Shizuoka|it|Atami|ja|熱海市|ko|아타미시|lt|Atamis|mg|Atami|ms|Atami, Shizuoka|mzn|آتامی، شیزوئوکا|nl|Atami|pl|Atami|pt|Atami|ro|Atami|ru|Атами|sv|Atami|tg|Атами|th|อาตามิ|tl|Atami|tr|Atami|tt|Атами|tum|Atami|uk|Атамі (Сідзуока)|ur|اٹامی|vi|Atami, Shizuoka|war|Atami, Shizuoka|zh|熱海市|zh_classical|熱海市|zh_min_nan|Atami-chhī|zh_yue|熱海|qid=Q653364|lt=Atami City}}. It is reputed to be one of the {{ill|Japan's Top 3|ja|日本三大一覧|zh|日本三大列表|qid=Q10311536|lt=Three Great Onsen}} of Japan.
== Water Quality ==
* Sodium–Calcium Chloride Spring – 80%
* Sodium–Calcium Chloride–Sulfate Spring – 19%
* Sodium–Calcium Sulfate Spring – 1%
** 18,000 liters per minute discharge rate
** A colorless, transparent {{ill|source|ja|源泉|ko|원천 (온천)|qid=Q11564196}}
** A total of 410 sources (over 600 including those from Izu-yama and Amishiro)
** A high-temperature spring with a discharge temperature of 98.2°C
The majority of the sources are {{ill|Brine spring|de|Solequelle|ja|塩化物泉|nn|Saltbrønn|qid=Q11428612|lt=Brine spring}}. Along the mountainsides, many sources are {{ill|Sulfate spring|ja|硫酸塩泉|qid=Q11587674}}. In ancient times, most sources were of the sulfate type. However, due to extensive source development by {{ill|Boring (earth)|ar|حفر (الأرض)|be|Бурэнне|de|Bohrung (Geologie)|fa|حفاری (زمین)|hi|वेधन (पृथ्वी)|hy|Հորատապայթեցման աշխատանքներ|ja|ボーリング|kk|Бұрғылау|ko|시추 (토공)|lv|Zemes urbšana|pl|Odwiert|ru|Бурение|tr|Sondaj|uk|Буріння|qid=Q12177444|lt=Borehole drilling}}, an increased amount of {{ill|Seawater|en|Seawater|qid=Q184395|lt=seawater}} mixed into the underground veins led to a change in the {{ill|water quality|ja|泉質}}.
In the past, sources located near the {{ill|Tōkaidō Main Line|ja|Tōkaidō Main Line|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135502397}} tracks were of the chloride–sulfate type, but since the later Shōwa period many have shifted to being predominantly chloride springs.
Compared with neutral chloride springs in other prefectures, the higher sulfate content makes the water slightly alkaline, resulting in a smoother feel on the skin.
== Hot Spring Town ==
[[File:Atami Iyeyasu hot spring.jpg|thumb|{{ill|Atami Iyeyasu hot spring|ja|家康の湯|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135493085}}]]
[[File:Atami 01.jpg|thumb|Souvenir shops in the hot spring town]]
[[File:Great Fire of Atami.JPG|thumb|Thumbnail|The Atami Ginza Shopping Street burned down in the 1950 {{ill|Atami Great Fire|ja|熱海大火|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q131919958}}]]
At the northeastern tip of the {{ill|Izu Peninsula|en|Izu Peninsula|qid=Q822822|lt=Izu Peninsula}}, along the seacoast facing the {{ill|Sagami Bay|ja|相模灘|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 相模湾|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1061221}}, from the northeast to the southeast of {{ill|Atami Station|en|Atami Station|qid=Q800412|lt=Atami Station}}, a row of ryokan and hotels stretches along the coast. Facilities seeking scenic views are also built on the mountainside. The traditional {{ill|Spa town|en|Spa town|qid=Q4946461|lt=Onsen town}} has long spread from the station area at the foot of the mountain to the seacoast. The tourist area includes the shopping complex {{ill|Atami Station|ja|ラスカ熱海|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熱海駅|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q800412}}, the shopping street near the station, attractions such as {{ill|Kiunkaku|ja|起雲閣|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11636134}}, seashore bathing facilities, and further to the south, locations such as {{ill|Nishikigaura|ja|錦ヶ浦|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11650415}}, {{ill|Atami Castle|en|Atami Castle|qid=Q11257168|lt=Atami Castle}}, and even the island of {{ill|Hatsushima|en|Hatsushima|qid=Q689643|lt=Hatsushima}}, making it a comprehensive tourist destination.
{{ill|Atami Station|en|Atami Station|qid=Q800412|lt=Atami Station}} is the first station on the {{ill|Itō Line|en|Itō Line|qid=Q1049129|lt=Itō Line}} and serves as a gateway to Izu tourism in the east.

=== Atami Nanayu (Seven Onsen of Atami) ===
The hot spring town once featured seven natural sources, known as '''Atami Nanayu''' (熱海七湯), dating back to the Edo period; however, due to the impact of subsequent source development from the Meiji period onward, the natural discharge of these springs was lost. The source known as {{ill|Ōyu|ja|大湯|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11437542}} was restored as an artificial geyser in 1962 (Shōwa 37), while the other six were restored in 1997 (Heisei 9) as cultural and tourist resources by artificially inducing municipal hot spring discharge.<ref>[http://www.city.atami.lg.jp/kanko/onsen/1001823.html Atami Nanayu Tour] - Atami City</ref>
The Seven Onsen of Atami are as follows:
* '''Ōyu''' (大湯, also known as {{ill|Ōyu Geyser|ja|大湯間歇泉|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q65258433}}) – formerly the central source of Atami Onsen.
* '''Nonaka no Yu''' (野中の湯) – located to the east of {{ill|Fujimori Inari Shrine|ja|藤森稲荷神社|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135502426}}, with visible steam.
* '''Kosawa no Yu''' (小沢の湯) – named after its locality; situated to the north behind the {{ill|Shizuoka Bank|en|Shizuoka Bank|qid=Q7499501|lt=Shizuoka Bank}} Atami branch along Onsen Street; its high-temperature steam is even used to boil eggs. A drinking fountain for water from the {{ill|Tanna Tunnel|ja|丹那湧水}} is also provided.
* '''Furo no Yu''' (風呂の湯) – located adjacent to {{ill|Fukushima-ya Ryokan|ja|福島屋旅館}}, usually paired with {{ill|Mizu no Yu|ja|水の湯}}.
* '''Me no Yu''' (目の湯) – named for its reputed healing properties; located along Ginza-dōri between {{ill|Suruga Bank|ja|スルガ銀行|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11313470}} and {{ill|Shizuoka Chuo Bank|ja|静岡中央銀行|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11662920}}; formerly also known as '''Sajirō no Yu''' (佐治郎の湯) after its former owner.
* '''Seizaemon no Yu''' (清左右衛門の湯) – named after a deceased farmer; located west of {{ill|Furutani Ryokan|ja|古谷旅館}}, with visible steam.
* '''Kawahara Yu''' (河原湯) – formerly a source for the common people, located on a riverside at Higashihama; situated along {{ill|Japan National Route 135|en|Japan National Route 135|qid=Q6156779|lt=National Route 135}} near the southern end of the Seven Onsen; note the nearby convenience store.

==== Ōyu Geyser ====
{{main|Ōyu Geyser}}
[[File:Geyser in Atami.jpg|thumb|Atami’s geyser in the Meiji era]]
[[File:230127 Oyu Atami Onsen Atami Japan02s3.jpg|thumb|Ōyu Geyser<br />(The current one is artificial)]]
The {{ill|Ōyu Geyser|ja|大湯間歇泉|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q65258433}} was once reputed to be one of the world’s three major {{ill|Geyser|en|Geyser|qid=Q83471|lt=geyser}}<nowiki/>s, but due to extensive drilling in the surrounding area after the Meiji period, its natural discharge diminished and it no longer erupts spontaneously. It is now maintained as an artificial geyser.
In the past, it erupted several times per day; records from the late Edo period counted up to eight eruptions per day, but its frequency decreased during the Meiji period.<ref name="takayanagi">Tomohiko Takayanagi,  ''Rekishi to Keizai'' 2006, Vol.48, Issue 3, pp.41–58, {{doi|10.20633/rekishitokeizai.48.3_41}}</ref>
Conflicts arose between advocates for preserving Ōyu and factions seeking to expand the hot spring town beyond it. In 1883, records indicate that eruptions occurred three times during both day and night.<ref name=takayanagi/>
Around 1902 (mid-Meiji period), spontaneous eruptions ceased. Alarmed, local residents commissioned physicist [[Honda Kōtarō|Honda Kōtarō]] who, with his assistant [[:en:Terada Torahiko|Terada Torahiko]], succeeded in restoring the geyser.<ref>Atsushi Katsuki, [https://hdl.handle.net/2433/89730 Honda’s Magnetic Theory and the Acceptance Process of Weiss Theory in Japan: Based on Oral Accounts] ''Bussō Kenkyū'' 1978, Vol.31, Issue 1, pp.1– (Bussō Kenkyūkai)</ref>
At that time, the geyser erupted on average four times per day for about eight minutes each.<ref>[[Kozu Sotsuyū]], [https://doi.org/10.5026/jgeography.24.754 Atami Onsen Survey Report] ''Chigaku Zasshi'' 1912, Vol.24, Issue 11, pp.754–764, {{doi|10.5026/jgeography.24.754}}</ref>
Later, in Taishō 12, spontaneous eruptions ceased and the source became depleted, prompting the lifting of drilling restrictions and a surge in drilling on the mountainside and reclaimed coastal areas; by Shōwa 10, as many as 220 wells had been drilled. However, new drilling was later suspended; during a 1912 survey by [[Kozu Sotsuyū|Kozu Sotsuyū]], the average eruption had declined to about two eruptions per day, each lasting three minutes.
After the Great Kantō Earthquake, spontaneous eruptions resumed briefly but ceased again in the early Shōwa period. Finally, in 1962 (Shōwa 37), the municipal hot spring system was used to pump water, and an artificial geyser was established, which remains in operation today.
A replica of Japan’s first {{ill|Payphone|en|Payphone|qid=Q900977|lt=public telephone}} box has been installed near the annex of the {{ill|Atami New Fujiya Hotel|ja|熱海ニューフジヤホテル|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11569074}}.
Additionally, a monument commemorates [[Rutherford Allcock]], the first recorded British envoy to reach the summit of {{ill|Mount Fuji|en|Mount Fuji|qid=Q39231|lt=Mount Fuji}} during the Bakumatsu period, and the grave of his Scottish Terrier Toby, who accompanied him, suffered severe burns at this geyser on his return journey, and later died there. Although Toby received extensive care from local residents, he ultimately passed away. The grave was erected by local residents in mourning, and legend has it that Allcock expressed his gratitude; the tombstone bears the inscription “poor Toby (かわいそうなトビー)”.

== History ==
[[File:Zushu_atami_zenzu.jpg|alt=Full map of Atami Onsen from the Meiji era|thumb]]
[[File:Atami_Onsen_in_Taisho_era.jpg|alt=Taishō era|thumb]]
[[File:A_party_of_Japanese_visitors_at_the_hot_springs_resort_of_Atami,_near_Tokyo.jpg|alt=Shōwa era|thumb]]
[[File:View_of_Atami.JPG|alt=Year 2011|thumb]]
Atami is historically an ancient hot spring resort. It is said that about 1500 years ago, during the time of {{ill|Emperor Ninken|en|Emperor Ninken|qid=Q357266|lt=Emperor Ninken}}, boiling hot water gushed forth from the sea, causing fish to rot and die—a phenomenon discovered by local residents. Because of this, the place was named Atami, meaning “hot sea.”
Furthermore, there is a legend that during the {{ill|Tenpyō-hōji|en|Tenpyō-hōji|qid=Q1346307|lt=Tenpyō Hōji}} period, {{ill|Mangan|ja|万巻上人|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 万巻|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11353818}} of {{ill|Hakone Gongen|ja|箱根権現}}, in order to relieve fishermen suffering from poor catches caused by this “hot sea,” prayed and transferred the source from the sea to its present location in the mountain village.<ref>{{Cite web|和書|url=http://www.city.atami.shizuoka.jp/page.php?p_id=1100|title=熱海の温泉|publisher=熱海市役所|accessdate=2016-04-10}}</ref>
During the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|en|Nanboku-chō period|qid=Q264012|lt=Nanboku-chō period}}, in {{ill|Ōan|en|Ōan|qid=Q1146245|lt=Ōan era}}7/{{ill|Bunchū|en|Bunchū|qid=Q1194181|lt=Bunchū era}}3 ({{ill|1374|en|1374|qid=Q6269|lt=1374 AD}}), on March 4, a Kamakura native, {{ill|Gidō Shūshin|en|Gidō Shūshin|qid=Q1335613|lt=Gidō Shūshin}}, visited Atami Onsen. He noted in his diary that a poetry gathering had been held on the occasion of the {{ill|Double Third Festival|en|Double Third Festival|qid=Q698091|lt=Shōmatsuri Festival (March 3)}}, at which he composed {{ill|Shi (poetry)|en|Shi (poetry)|qid=Q1759242|lt=Chinese poetry}} (as recorded in the ''{{ill|Kūka Nichiyō Kōfuryaku-shū|ja|空華日用工夫略集}}'', entry for Ōan 7, March 4). This record not only indicates that many literati frequented Atami at the time but also is known as an anecdote concerning the discrepancy between the dates of the {{ill|Kyō calendar|ja|京暦}} used in Kyoto and the {{ill|Mishima calendar|ja|三島暦|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11355249}} used in Atami.<ref>桃裕行「京暦と三島暦との日の食違いについて」『桃裕行著作集』第8巻、詩文閣出版、1990th year 、P223-230.（原論文:『天文総報』第14巻4号、1960th year 4月）</ref>
In the early {{ill|Edo period|ar|فترة إيدو|ast|Periodu Edo|az|Edo dövrü|bcl|Panahon nin Edo|be|Перыяд Эда|bg|Едо (период)|bn|এদো যুগ|bo|ཨེ་དོའི་དུས་སྐབས།|br|Marevezh Edo|ca|Període Edo|ckb|سەردەمی ئێدۆ|cs|Období Edo|cv|Эдо тапхăрĕ|da|Edo-perioden|de|Edo-Zeit|eo|Epoko de Edo|es|Período Edo|et|Edo ajastu|eu|Edo aroa|fa|دوره ادو|fi|Edo-kausi|fr|Époque d'Edo|gl|Período Edo|he|תקופת אדו|hi|एदो अवधी|hr|Edo (razdoblje)|hu|Edo-kor|id|Zaman Edo|is|Jedótímabilið|it|Periodo Edo|ja|江戸時代|jv|Jaman Édo|ko|에도 시대|lt|Edo laikotarpis|lv|Edo periods|mk|Едо (период)|mn|Эдогийн эрин|ms|Zaman Edo|nl|Edoperiode|nn|Edotida|oc|Periòde Edo|pl|Edo (okres)|pt|Período Edo|ro|Perioada Edo|ru|Период Эдо|simple|Edo period|sk|Obdobie Edo|sl|Obdobje Edo|sq|Periudha Edo|sr|Едо период|su|Période Edo|sv|Edoperioden|th|ยุคเอโดะ|tl|Panahong Edo|tok|tenpo pi kulupu lawa Eto|tr|Edo Dönemi|uk|Період Едо|ur|ایڈو دور|uz|Edo davri|vi|Thời kỳ Edo|war|Panahon Edo|wuu|江戶時代|zh|江户时代|zh_min_nan|Edo sî-tāi|zh_yue|江戶時代|qid=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}, in the 9th year of the {{ill|Keichō|en|Keichō|qid=Q1328185|lt=Keichō era}} (1604), {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|qid=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu}} stayed for seven days for {{ill|Thermal bath|ja|湯治|2=ja|3=湯治|4=zh|5=湯治|6=ca|7=Termalisme|8=de|9=Thermalbad|10=es|11=Termalismo|13=Thermal bath|14=eo|15=Varmfonta banejo|16=fr|17=Thermalisme|18=la|19=Balneum thermale|20=lb|21=Thermalbad|22=hu|23=Termálfürdő|24=nl|25=Thermaalbad|26=pt|27=Turismo termal|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1004887}} (hot spring treatment), as recorded in the ''{{ill|Tokugawa jikki|ja|徳川実紀|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q2439031}}''. Since then, as a famed hot spring favored by the {{ill|Tokugawa shogunate|ja|徳川将軍家|lt=Tokugawa Shogunate}} and its {{ill|Royal warrant of appointment|en|Royal warrant of appointment|qid=Q1070771|lt=Officially Patronized}}, from the time of {{ill|Tokugawa Iemitsu|en|Tokugawa Iemitsu|qid=Q314481|lt=Tokugawa Iemitsu}} onward, Atami’s hot spring water was presented to Edo Castle through the "Gokyu-yu" ceremony.<ref>{{Cite book|和書 |title=熱海錦嚢 |year=1897|publisher=芹沢政吉 |author=斎藤要人 |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/pid/764830/1/32}}</ref>
After the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}} period, many literati visited Atami, and numerous works were set in this locale. The most representative work is {{ill|Konjiki Yasha|ja|金色夜叉|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11647825}} by {{ill|Ozaki Kōyō|en|Ozaki Kōyō|qid=Q975273|lt=Ozaki Kōyō}}, through which Atami became known nationwide. Along {{ill|Japan National Route 135|en|Japan National Route 135|qid=Q6156779|lt=National Route 135}}, statues of the characters Kan'ichi and Omiya can be found. Other notable works include {{ill|Winter Day|ja|冬の日|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11395202}} by {{ill|Kafū Nagai|en|Kafū Nagai|qid=Q530588|lt=Nagai Kafū}} and {{ill|Uzushio|ja|うず潮|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to うずしお|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q16874528}} by {{ill|Fumiko Hayashi (author)|en|Fumiko Hayashi (author)|qid=Q445839|lt=Hayashi Fumiko}}. In 1923 (Taishō 12), Atami suffered significant damage during the {{ill|aftermath of 1923 Great Kantō earthquake|ja|関東大震災|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q3742341}}, but with the extension of Atami Station on the {{ill|Tōkaidō Main Line|ja|熱海線|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 東海道本線|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1190152}} of the national railway the following year, the area quickly recovered; on July 1, 1936 (Shōwa 11), the Atami Town-operated Onsen (later City-operated Onsen) was established.<ref>[https://www.city.atami.lg.jp/kurashi/suido/1004882/1005368.html "市営温泉のはじまり]</ref>
At that time, Atami was such a thriving hot spring resort that newspapers described it as "a town of eroticism, a town of {{ill|jokyū café|ja|カフェー (風俗営業)|lt=Cafe|lt_ja=カフェー|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11294599}}," reflecting the booming {{ill|Mores|ja|風俗産業|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 風俗|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1115221}}. However, in {{ill|1934|en|1934|qid=Q18714|lt=1934 AD}} (Shōwa 9), when the {{ill|Tanna Tunnel|en|Tanna Tunnel|qid=Q7683603|lt=Tanna Tunnel}} opened and tourists flocked to the hot springs, many cafes were converted into dining establishments.<ref>開通後初の正月に伊豆の温泉は超満員『東京日日新聞』昭和10th year 1月8日（『昭和ニュース事典第5巻 昭和10th year -昭和11th year 』本編p363 昭和ニュース事典編纂委員会 毎日コミュニケーションズ刊 1994th year )</ref>
In the postwar period of turmoil, a {{ill|Panpan girls|ja|パンパン|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11329737}} emerged, characterized by a decline in public morals and catering to occupation army soldiers, among others.<ref>[https://www.aozora.gr.jp/cards/001095/files/43178_21390.html]{{ill|Aozora Bunko|en|Aozora Bunko|qid=Q83466|lt=Aozora Bunko}}</ref>
Subsequently, Atami suffered great damage in the {{ill|Atami Great Fire|ja|熱海大火|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q131919958}}, but during the Shōwa 30s it became a prime destination for honeymoon trips, bustling with couples ({{ill|Couple (relationship)|ja|カップル|lt=Abecc|lt_ja=アベック|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q219160}} recognizable by their white dresses and white suitcases). After the opening of the {{ill|Tokaido Shinkansen|en|Tokaido Shinkansen|qid=Q660895|lt=Tōkaidō Shinkansen}}, in the Shōwa 40s, the impact of the {{ill|Japanese economic miracle|en|Japanese economic miracle|qid=Q1059474|lt=High Economic Growth Period}} led to a focus on attracting {{ill|group tours|ja|団体旅行|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11420283}}, and visitors from not only the Kantō region but also from the {{ill|Chūkyō metropolitan area|en|Chūkyō metropolitan area|qid=Q1377209|lt=Chukyo}} and {{ill|Kansai region|en|Kansai region|qid=Q164256|lt=Kansai}} increased, with the number of overnight guests exceeding 4.5 million annually.<ref name="sankei20180902">[https://www.sankei.com/article/20180827-FO6IEV7LEFO7BIFPCMMRG5DI34/ “Atami Revival: A Successful Community-wide Effort in Town Revitalization” {{ill|Sankei Shimbun|en|Sankei Shimbun|qid=Q1197261|lt=Sankei Shimbun}}, morning edition, September 2, 2018 (comprehensive), viewed September 19, 2018]</ref> During the bubble era, soaring land prices in the {{ill|Special wards of Tokyo|en|Special wards of Tokyo|qid=Q308891|lt=Tokyo metropolitan area}} and the spread of {{ill|Shinkansen commuting|ja|新幹線通勤|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11502167}} led to many high-income individuals building homes with hot springs in Atami and commuting to Tokyo via the Shinkansen.
However, due to the {{ill|Lost Decades|en|Lost Decades|qid=Q1141122|lt=bubble collapse}}, corporate resort facilities and group tours declined, and with the generalization of {{ill|international tourism in Japan|ja|海外旅行|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q120334380}} amid a {{ill|Japanese Yen rate|ja|円高|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 円相場|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11394831}}, the number of visitors from distant regions—including from Kansai—dropped. Moreover, a series of earthquakes off the coast of Ito in the early 1990s further compounded the decline in tourism, and in 2006, Atami City even declared a fiscal crisis.<ref>[https://www.travelvoice.jp/20201108-147348 衰退から一転、「熱海の奇跡」が実現した舞台裏を、再生キーパーソンに聞いてきた　―街づくりと観光の連動から「関係人口」の創出まで｜トラベルボイス（観光産業ニュース）]</ref>
In response, local volunteers began to take action.<ref>[https://gendai.media/articles/-/56405 衰退一途の熱海がいつのまにか復活を遂げた「再生の秘密」（市来 広一郎） | 現代ビジネス | 講談社（1/4） ]</ref> In the Atami Ginza Shopping Street, which connects Atami Station with the ryokan and hotel district, vacant storefronts that had proliferated were revitalized through efforts by {{ill|U-turn|en|U-turn|qid=Q1343116|lt=U-turn}} returnees from Tokyo, local residents, and the city’s initiative to hold open-air markets and attract enterprising shop owners through business model transformations.
Thus, the long-term downward trend bottomed out in 2011 and reversed, drawing attention as the “Atami Revival.” The inherent advantage of being located adjacent to a Shinkansen station in the western part of the {{ill|Greater Tokyo Area|en|Greater Tokyo Area|qid=Q328121|lt=Metropolitan Area}} remains intact, and the ryokan and hotel industries have succeeded by enhancing their appeal to individual and small-group travelers through events such as {{ill|Fireworks|ja|花火大会|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 花火|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q127933|lt=fireworks}}.<ref>[https://president.jp/articles/-/23322 なぜ「熱海」は人気観光地に返り咲いたか アラフィフのおじさんたちが大奮闘] {{ill|President|ja|プレジデント社|lt=President Online|lt_ja=プレジデント・オンライン|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11335839}} (October 12, 2017) viewed September 19, 2018]</ref>
=== History of Hotels ===
* November 30, 1976 (Shōwa 51): A fire broke out at the {{ill|Atami Rinkai Hotel|ja|熱海臨海ホテル|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135502429}}, resulting in 2 casualties.
* Around 1990 (Heisei 2): Following the {{ill|Lost Decades|en|Lost Decades|qid=Q1141122|lt=bubble collapse}}, group tourism declined significantly. Many large ryokan that did not target individual customers closed in succession, giving the town a deserted impression and further accelerating the loss of guests.
* August 30, 1999 (Heisei 11): SF Shōji, which operated both the {{ill|Atami Fujiya Hotel|ja|熱海富士屋ホテル|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135502431}} and the {{ill|Atami 11 Fujiya Hotel|ja|熱海ニュー富士屋ホテル|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135502433}}, applied for corporate rehabilitation with debts amounting to 99 billion yen.
* October 1, 1999 (Heisei 11): {{ill|Dankaisō|ja|暖海荘}} filed for bankruptcy with debts of 126 billion yen.
* 2000 (Heisei 12): The operator of {{ill|Kiunkaku|ja|起雲閣|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11636134}}, {{ill|Japan Tourism Co., Ltd.|ja|日本観光株式会社}}, went bankrupt with debts of 192 billion yen.
* 2001 (Heisei 13): The long-established, large ryokan {{ill|Tsuruya Hotel|ja|つるやホテル (熱海温泉)|lt=Tsuruya Hotel|lt_ja=つるやホテル|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q60987069}} ceased operations.
* 2004 (Heisei 16): {{ill|Atami Kinjōkan|ja|熱海金城館}} filed for bankruptcy with debts of 31 billion yen.
* 2006 (Heisei 18): The venerable, large hotel {{ill|Ōtsuki Hotel|ja|大月ホテル|qid=Q140447138}} applied for corporate rehabilitation with debts of 46 billion yen. At that time, facilities closed in the following order—Ōtsuki Hotel, Tsuruya Hotel, Dankaisō, {{ill|Atami Grand Hotel|ja|熱海グランドホテル|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135502437}}, {{ill|Hotel 11 Yamato|ja|ホテル ニュー大和|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135502440}}, and {{ill|Atami Rinkai Hotel|ja|熱海臨海ホテル|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135502429}}—resulting in an eerie landscape of abandoned ruins.
* May 15, 2008 (Heisei 20): {{ill|Womizaki Hotel|ja|ウオミサキホテル|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135502442}} filed for personal bankruptcy at the Numazu branch of the Shizuoka District Court with debts of 23.5 billion yen.
* May 2010 (Heisei 22): The operator of {{ill|Okamoto Hotel|ja|岡本ホテル|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135502444}}, {{ill|Okamoto Club|ja|岡本倶楽部|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q55535752}}, went bankrupt. Later, those involved were punished for violations of the {{ill|Act on Punishment of Organized Crimes and Control of Proceeds of Crime|ja|組織的な犯罪の処罰及び犯罪収益の規制等に関する法律|lt=Organized Crime Punishment Act|lt_ja=組織犯罪処罰法|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11606344}}.<ref>{{Cite web|和書|date=2013-05-30|url=https://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXNASDG30014_Q3A530C1CC0000/|title=岡本ホテル事件、実質オーナーに懲役18th year 　東京地裁判決|publisher=日本経済新聞|accessdate=2018-06-22}}</ref>
* November 19, 2010 (Heisei 22): {{ill|Ōnoya|ja|大野屋|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11439581}} applied for corporate rehabilitation at the Numazu branch of the Shizuoka District Court with debts of 21.5 billion yen.
* February 25, 2011 (Heisei 23): The employee dormitory of {{ill|Shihomiya Ryokan|ja|志ほみや旅館|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135502446}} was completely destroyed by fire; fortunately, proper evacuation prevented any injuries.
* October 15, 2011 (Heisei 23): {{ill|Nanmei Hotel|ja|南明ホテル|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135502449}} filed for personal bankruptcy at the Numazu branch of the Shizuoka District Court with debts of 17 billion yen.
* July 28, 2018 (Heisei 30): Due to a storm surge from Typhoon No. 12, the restaurant windows of {{ill|Hotel New Akao|ja|ホテルニューアカオ|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ACAO SPA & RESORT|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q63801636}} were broken.
* July 3, 2021 (Reiwa 3): {{ill|Atami 11 Fujiya Hotel|ja|熱海ニュー富士屋ホテル|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135502433}} and {{ill|Hotel New Akao|ja|ホテルニューアカオ|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ACAO SPA & RESORT|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q63801636}} served as evacuation shelters for victims of the {{ill|2021 Atami landslide|en|2021 Atami landslide|qid=Q107405872|lt=Atami City Izu Mountain Debris Flow Disaster}}.
== Byword for Entertainment Districts ==
Because Atami Onsen once flourished as Japan’s representative entertainment hot spring, similar or famous {{ill|Spa town|en|Spa town|qid=Q4946461|lt=Onsen town}}s and {{ill|onsenkyō|ja|温泉郷|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11562971}}s in other regions have been advertised as “the Atami of ○○” or referred to as such.
Similarly, these hot spring towns, like Atami Onsen, have experienced a decline in visitors due to factors such as the collapse of the bubble economy and the diversification of {{ill|Leisure|en|Leisure|qid=Q180910|lt=Leisure}}, and there are now instances where existing hot spring towns are described in contexts such as “the XX Onsen that was once called the Atami of ○○ …”<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.mutusinpou.co.jp/%E6%B4%A5%E8%BB%BD%E3%81%AE%E8%A1%97%E3%81%A8%E9%A2%A8%E6%99%AF/2015/03/35640.html|title=Asamushi Onsen Becomes an Entertainment District|newspaper={{ill|Mutsu Shinpo|ja|陸奥新報|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11658598}}|publisher={{ill|Mutsu Shinpo|ja|陸奥新報社|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 陸奥新報|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11658598}}|date=2015-3-23|author=Miho Nakazono (Researcher, Aomori Prefectural History Compilation)|accessdate=2015-11-28}}</ref><ref>Example of Asamushi Onsen being called “the Atami of Tōhoku” – ‘{{ill|Kahoku Shimpō|en|Kahoku Shimpō|qid=Q639774|lt=Kahoku Shimpo}}’ August 11, 1994.</ref>
On the other hand, there are cases such as {{ill|Kaike Onsen|ja|皆生温泉|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11580978}}, which brands itself as “the Atami of the {{ill|San'in region|en|San'in region|qid=Q398310|lt=San'in}},” using the term as a straightforward promotional slogan without any negative or passive connotations.
In a special case, {{ill|Bandai Atami Onsen|ja|磐梯熱海温泉|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11587893}} was so named because the lord at the time of its opening was originally from Izu, and thus it has become a name closely associated with the local area.
== Closed Facilities ==
<div class="NavFrame" style="width:100%;">
 <div class="NavHead" style="padding:1.5px; line-height:1.7; letter-spacing:1px;">Closed Facilities</div>
 <div class="NavContent" style="text-align:left;">
* Atami Grand Hotel  
Higashi-kaigan-cho, Atami City  
Closed in 1995. It had become a ruin, but was demolished in 2003.
* Hotel Ichifuji  
9-2, Sakimachi, Atami City  
Demolished around 1996, and a condominium "Atami City Villa Sakimachi" was constructed in its place.
* Hotel Atamikaku  
4-16, Taharamoto-cho, Atami City  
Currently in operation under the management of Itoen Hotel.
* Hotel Dankaisou  
12, Higashi-kaigan-cho, Atami City  
Declared bankrupt in 1999 with debts of 12 billion yen. It was demolished. The land was auctioned, and although the Manyo Group planned to purchase it and construct a hotel, the plan was scrapped.
* Isobenkai  
3-8, Sakimachi, Atami City  
It has become known as "Sophia Atami Deisas."
* Kiunkaku  
4-2, Shōwa-cho, Atami City  
In 1999, its operating company, Japan Kankō, went bankrupt with debts of 19.2 billion yen. Subsequently, it came under the management of Atami City and is open to the public.
* Shōtō Main Building  
5-30, Wadahama Minamimachi, Atami City  
Closed in 1999; later became a ruin and was demolished in 2016.
* Atami 11 Fujiya Hotel  
1-16, Ginza-cho, Atami City  
In 1999, its operating company, SF Shōji, went bankrupt with debts of 9.9 billion yen. In 2006, it was acquired by Itoen Hotel and resumed operations.
* Atami Fujiya Hotel  
13-18, Ginza-cho, Atami City  
In 1999, its operating company, SF Shōji, went bankrupt with debts of 9.9 billion yen, leading to its closure and demolition. A condominium, "Lebens Resort Atami," was constructed in its place.
* Atami Rinkai Hotel  
11-24, Higashi-kaigan-cho, Atami City  
On November 30, 1976, a fire occurred causing fatal burns. It went bankrupt in 2000. Around 2007, it was demolished and became the condominium "Zephyr Atami Beach Tower."
* Atami Onsen Hotel  
4-6, Sakimachi  
Formerly a rest facility for Tokyo Metropolitan Government employees, it closed at the end of May 2001. It was later renovated and reopened as "Hotel Aiola," but then closed again. It is currently operating as "Yumeiroha."
* Atami Kankō Hotel  
2-11, Taharamoto-cho, Atami City  
Closed at the end of June 2001. It was demolished, and a condominium "Leaage Atami" was built in its place.
* Tsuruya Hotel  
6-45, Higashi-kaigan-cho, Atami City  
Closed at the end of November 2001. It was demolished around 2005, and a multi-purpose building "Aune Atami" was constructed but went bankrupt during construction. After being left abandoned for 10 years, it reopened in 2020 as the "Atami Pearl Star Hotel" under foreign capital.
* Isobenkai  
2-13, Higashi-kaigan-cho, Atami City  
Ceased operations in December 2001. It was demolished and became the condominium "Duopia Atami."
* Atami 11 Asahi  
7-10, Higashi-kaigan-cho, Atami City  
Bankrupted around 2002. It was demolished around 2006, and in 2012, a members-only hotel "Tokyu Vacations Atami" was constructed.
* Atami Kinjōkan  
10-33, Shōwa-cho, Atami City  
Declared bankrupt in November 2004 with debts of 3.1 billion yen. Subsequently, it became part of the Itoen Hotel group and resumed operations.
* Ōtsuki Hotel (First Generation)  
3-19, Higashi-kaigan-cho, Atami City  
At the end of May 2006, it went bankrupt with debts of 4.6 billion yen. Later, with capital participation from Orix, it resumed operations.
* Nishi-Atami Hotel  
1-1, Umezono-cho, Atami City  
A hotel operated by Izuhakone Railway that closed at the end of August 2006. It was demolished around 2010 and became a condominium.
* Kokumin Shukusha Atami Village  
21-7, Umezono-cho, Atami City  
Closed on January 15, 2008. It is currently operated by Daiichi Kōshō Co., Ltd. as the lodging facility "Utayuno Yado Atami Shiki Hotel."
* Womizaki Hotel  
7-2, Wadahama Minamimachi, Atami City  
Declared bankrupt in May 2008 with debts of 2.35 billion yen. Later that same year, it was acquired by Itoen Hotel and resumed operations.
* Atami Okamoto Hotel  
1, Kamiyado-cho, Atami City  
Closed in 2010 due to the bankruptcy of the Okamoto Group. It was later demolished, and a public facility is planned to be built on the site.
* Atami Hotel Kaizan  
11-19, Higashi-kaigan-cho, Atami City  
Bankrupted and closed in 2010. Currently, the new building is used as a camp facility for group driving license training by a driving school.
* Hotel Ōnoya  
3-9, Wadahama Minamimachi, Atami City  
Declared bankrupt in November 2010 with debts of 2.15 billion yen. Subsequently, it came under the umbrella of Itoen Hotel and resumed operations.
* Nanmei Hotel  
8-3, Sakimachi, Atami City  
Declared bankrupt in November 2011 with debts of 1.7 billion yen. Afterwards, Ōedo Onsen Monogatari acquired the hotel and reopened it as "Ōedo Onsen Monogatari Atami."
* Hotel South Bay  
6-49, Higashi-kaigan-cho, Atami City  
Originally an annex of Nanmei Hotel, it ceased operations in 2011 following Nanmei Hotel's bankruptcy and has since been left abandoned.
* Shiroki Ryokan  
7-6, Nagisacho, Atami City  
Ceased operations at the end of January 2012, was demolished, and later became a condominium.
* Hotel Ikeda  
12-40, Higashi-kaigan-cho, Atami City  
Ceased operations on January 21, 2012, and was demolished.
* SS Seiyaku Atami Retreat  
(Closed around 1990)  
Later became a retreat facility for Jonan Shinyokinko, but closed again around 2014. Since 2015, it has been operating as "Atami Fuga."
